title: Display-fab DRAM: oxide 1T1C arrays on Gen-8.5 glass panels
idea: Borrowed from LCD/OLED backplane fabs: run IGZO 1T1C memory tiles on idle Gen-8.5 (2.2x2.5 m) glass lines, which pattern ~1-1.5 um features with cheap panel steppers at a few $/cm2, deposit 4-8 oxide tiers per panel, then dice into tiles flip-bonded over a small CMOS periphery die.
why: Capital intensity and idle-capacity reuse: depreciated display fabs cost ~50x less per processed cm2 than 300 mm DRAM lines; density is 10x+ worse per tier, so it only pays as a slow bulk tier or with many stacked tiers.

title: Solar spatial-ALD conveyor for DRAM capacitor stacks
idea: Borrowed from solar PERC lines, which deposit AlOx by spatial ALD: wafers move under fixed slots of precursor, purge and oxidant at near-atmospheric pressure, so pulses become positions instead of time steps. Adapt a rotary spatial-ALD platen to DRAM ZrO2/Al2O3/TiN capacitor stacks, removing the vacuum purge cycles that dominate cluster-tool time.
why: Facts 1/4: capacitor-stack ALD is among the slowest, most tool-heavy array steps; spatial ALD claims 5-10x throughput per tool and ~3x lower capex per wafer pass, if conformality at AR 60+ holds.

title: Two-level nanoimprint stamp, like CD replication, for node and pad
idea: Borrowed from CD/DVD plants, which mold multi-depth pit structures in one shot: make a two-level quartz imprint template carrying both landing-pad and storage-node levels, so one jet-and-flash imprint replaces two critical exposures and their overlay step, the way dual damascene merged via and trench.
why: Fact 4: removes 1-2 EUV/193i-multipatterning layers per die from the array; NIL tool ~1/3 the price of EUV and self-aligned levels eliminate one overlay error budget.

title: HDD bit-patterned-media block copolymers quadruple capacitor hole density
idea: Borrowed from HDD bit-patterned-media R&D, which made 1 Tdot/in2 hexagonal dot arrays by guiding PS-b-PDMS block copolymers on sparse e-beam patterns. DRAM's storage-node array is the same hexagonal honeycomb: print a 4x-sparse guide with 193i, let a high-chi BCP fill the missing holes in each unit cell, then transfer by etch.
why: Fact 4: deletes the EUV or quad-patterning step for capacitor holes and gives a near-perfect lattice with low CD variation; needs defectivity below ~0.01/cm2.

title: Electrolytic-capacitor anodizing grows self-ordered 100:1 storage holes
idea: Borrowed from aluminum electrolytic capacitor foils and AAO filters, which self-organize hexagonal pores with AR >1000 just by anodizing aluminum in acid. Deposit thick Al over the cell array, seed pores on the landing-pad lattice by shallow pre-patterning, anodize straight down to any depth, then ALD electrode and dielectric into the alumina template.
why: Facts 1/4: the high-AR capacitor etch is the costliest array step; anodizing is a room-temperature wet bath with no plasma tool and no aspect-ratio-dependent etch slowdown. Pore ordering at <40 nm pitch is the risk.

title: Holographic grating writer: mask-free interference lithography for array lattices
idea: Borrowed from holographic diffraction-grating production, which uses interfering laser beams instead of masks. Because DRAM array layers (active, buried wordline, capacitor lattice) are strictly periodic, expose them with 3-6-beam 193 nm immersion interference at ~70 nm pitch, spacer-double to ~35 nm, and use one coarse trim exposure to cut array edges.
why: Fact 4: array critical layers become maskless and EUV-free; interference optics are simple (~1/10 scanner cost) with very high throughput.

title: Pottery bisque-then-glaze: capacitor-first flow, transistors on transferred silicon
idea: Borrowed from pottery, where the clay body is fired hot first and the glaze cooler later: build the capacitor array first with a 700-800 C crystallized SrTiO3 or rutile TiO2 dielectric (k~100), planarize, Smart-Cut-transfer a thin single-crystal Si film on top, then form access transistors at <=450 C with laser dopant activation.
why: Fact 1: unlocks k~100 dielectrics that need temperatures transistors cannot survive, so AR can drop from ~70 to ~35 for the same Cs, roughly halving capacitor etch cost and tool count.

title: Puff-pastry lamination: bond-thin-flip cycles double 3D DRAM tiers
idea: Borrowed from croissant dough, which gets 2^n layers by fold-and-roll: build a short 4-tier 3D DRAM block, hybrid-bond two such wafers face to face, thin one down to its tiers, and repeat on the doubled stack, so 4 to 8 to 16 to 32 tiers takes three bonding cycles instead of one 32-tier etch.
why: Fact 2: avoids the deep multi-tier etch and cumulative bow; every cycle reuses the same short process, so capex scales with bonders (~$5M) not high-AR etchers. Compounded bond yield is the risk.

title: Aircraft-leasing model for EUV and high-NA scanners
idea: Borrowed from aviation, where lessors like AerCap own about half of airline jets and redeploy them: a scanner lessor owns EUV tools, leases them per wafer pass to memory makers, moves tools between fabs as cycles shift, and funds itself with asset-backed securities on scanner residual value.
why: Fact 4: depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost; turning $200M+ tool capex into opex lowers entry cost for new or U.S. DRAM fabs and damps the boom-bust cycle.

title: Kalundborg-style fab symbiosis with neighboring heavy industry
idea: Borrowed from the Kalundborg industrial park, where plants trade steam, water and byproducts: site a DRAM fab beside a chlor-alkali plant (byproduct H2), a steel-mill air-separation unit (N2/O2/Ar), a data center that absorbs fab waste heat and a municipal water-reclaim plant, with pipelines replacing on-site gas yards and UPW pretreatment.
why: Capital, energy and water: on-site utilities are ~15-20% of fab capex; sharing could cut that by a third and shorten fab build time by months.

title: Optical-fiber preform drawing: coaxial capacitors drawn, bundled, sliced
idea: Borrowed from telecom fiber drawing and multimaterial fibers, which shrink a 10 cm preform 10,000x: draw a preform of packed coaxial metal/glass-dielectric/metal rods to ~50 nm cores, bundle and redraw, then slice the bundle into 1-5 um discs; each disc is a ready-made capacitor array, with aspect ratio set by slice thickness, bonded onto a transistor wafer.
why: Facts 1/4: zero lithography and zero high-AR etch for the capacitor, AR 100+ for free; core uniformity and registration to transistors are speculative.

title: Float-glass analog: silicon ribbon floated on molten metal
idea: Borrowed from Pilkington's float-glass process: pull a thin single-crystal silicon ribbon horizontally from a seed across a denser molten Sn-based bath under a barrier skin, producing 300 mm-wide wafer-thick sheet with no quartz crucible and no wire sawing, then grow a device-grade epi layer on top.
why: Scarce resource and cost: removes Spruce Pine HPQ crucibles and ~40% kerf loss; continuous growth could halve substrate cost. Metal contamination and crystal quality are high risk.

title: Cubic-zirconia skull melting: silicon grown inside its own frozen crust
idea: Borrowed from cubic-zirconia growth, where an RF-heated melt freezes against water-cooled copper fingers into its own container skin: apply cold-crucible induction melting to silicon crystal pulling, so a silicon skull holds the melt and no fused-quartz crucible is used.
why: Scarce resource: removes >80% Spruce Pine dependence; less oxygen in the crystal may also trim leakage-tail defects (Fact 3). Thermal-gradient control for 300 mm dislocation-free growth is the risk.

title: MLCC-in-a-hole: interleaved multi-electrode capacitor at low aspect ratio
idea: Borrowed from multilayer ceramic capacitors, which reach uF by stacking hundreds of interleaved electrodes: in a wider, shallower storage hole (AR ~20) ALD 4-6 alternating TiN/ZrO2 shells, then tie odd shells together at the bottom and even shells at the top with selective recess-and-cap, so capacitance multiplies with the number of dielectric layers.
why: Facts 1/4: 3-4x Cs per footprint without going to AR 115, relaxing the hardest etch; selective alternate-electrode contacting is the risky step.

title: Nanoporous-gold dealloying grows a sponge-surface storage electrode
idea: Borrowed from catalyst and supercapacitor makers, who leach the less-noble metal out of an alloy to get 10-50x surface area: deposit a Ru-Al alloy bottom electrode, dealloy the Al in mild base to leave porous Ru with 3-5 nm ligaments, then conformally coat dielectric and top electrode.
why: Fact 1: 2-3x effective electrode area gives AR-115-class charge at AR ~60; a metallic, low-resistance descendant of 1990s HSG silicon. Pore clogging inside a 20 nm node is high risk.

title: Miura-fold origami: one patterned membrane folded into 16 tiers
idea: Borrowed from origami solar arrays and Miura-fold maps: pattern 16 DRAM array tiles side by side in one planar pass on a 100 nm Si/oxide membrane with thin polymer hinge lines, release it, and fold it accordion-style onto a periphery die, with interconnect running across the hinges.
why: Fact 2: turns a 16-tier 3D process into one planar 2D process, ~16x fewer critical litho passes per bit; hinge wiring and stack flatness are speculative.

title: Cross-laminated timber: rotate tier orientation to cancel wafer bow
idea: Borrowed from cross-laminated timber, which rotates the grain 90 degrees per layer so warping cancels: in stacked 3D DRAM, rotate wordline/bitline direction 90 degrees every N tiers and alternate tensile and compressive film stacks so anisotropic stress cancels, keeping bow under ~50 um at 64+ tiers.
why: Fact 2: wafer bow and overlay drift cap tier count and force backside stress films and extra correction steps; stress cancellation buys more tiers per litho set.

title: Prestressed-concrete tendons keep tall capacitor pillars from leaning
idea: Borrowed from prestressed bridges, where tensioned steel keeps concrete in compression: deposit a tensile SiN/TiN liner inside each storage-node cylinder before the mold is removed, so pillars are pre-stressed straight and the multi-level support lattice can be dropped, letting AR reach 100-115 without collapse.
why: Fact 1: leaning and collapse cap capacitor height; dropping 1-2 support-layer litho/etch loops saves capex while raising Cs ~40%.

title: Steel minimill playbook: EUV-free DRAM on used DUV plus stacking
idea: Borrowed from Nucor's electric-arc minimills, which beat integrated mills starting with low-end rebar: build a $2-3B U.S. DRAM minimill on used ArF-immersion scanners at ~18-20 nm half-pitch with SAQP and no EUV, close the density gap by hybrid-bonding several array wafers over one periphery wafer, and sell first into industrial and auto DDR4/LPDDR4 that incumbents are exiting.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: ~5x less capex per wafer start than an EUV fab, with density recovered by stacking; enter low, move up.

title: LTPS excimer-laser crystallization builds polysilicon tiers at low temperature
idea: Borrowed from AMOLED backplanes, which turn amorphous Si into polysilicon with line-beam excimer lasers without heating the glass: deposit a-Si for each 3D DRAM tier and laser-crystallize it in nanoseconds, so tiers stack on finished CMOS and earlier tiers within BEOL thermal budgets.
why: Fact 2: the lateral transistor blocks 3D DRAM; display ELA tools already process 3 m2 glass, give ~100 cm2/Vs mobility and skip the costly Si/SiGe epitaxial superlattice.

title: Backside-power analogy: deep-trench capacitors etched from wafer backside
idea: Borrowed from logic backside power delivery and BSI image sensors: build transistors and bitlines on the front, bond to a carrier, thin to ~5 um, then etch deep-trench storage capacitors from the backside, landing on each transistor's source through nano-TSVs, so capacitors stop competing with bitline contacts for front-side space.
why: Facts 1/7: capacitor height is decoupled from front topology and the front area is freed for periphery; nano-TSV alignment at ~30 nm pitch is high risk.

title: MicroLED mass transfer: stamp-printed DRAM dielets onto logic wafers
idea: Borrowed from microLED displays, which move millions of 10 um LEDs at once with elastomer stamps: make 100x100 um DRAM array dielets on cheap mature-node wafers, undercut-release them, and transfer-print hundreds per die directly onto accelerator wafers beside the compute, wired with one redistribution layer.
why: Facts 5/6: near-memory without TSVs or HBM stacks; only known-good dielets get printed, lifting yield; transfer-print tools cost ~$5M versus TSV lines.

title: Par-baked bread: split DRAM front-end and finishing across fabs
idea: Borrowed from par-baked bread shipped from central bakeries to stores: leading fabs ship wafers with transistors, wordlines and bitlines done; regional U.S. finishing fabs add capacitors, top metals, test and packaging using only 193 nm dry litho, ALD and etch, splitting a ~90-day flow into two ~45-day hops.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: a finishing fab needs ~1/5 the capex and no EUV, captures ~40% of the process value and adds surge capacity close to customers.

title: Integrated-passive-device fabs supply ready-made trench capacitor wafers
idea: Borrowed from smartphone silicon capacitors (IPD trench caps, ~1 pF/um2) made in old 200 mm fabs: a 10-person team designs a cell-pitch trench-capacitor array, buys the wafers from an IPD foundry, buys transistor wafers from a foundry shuttle and has an OSAT hybrid-bond them; the team owns only design, integration and test.
why: Facts 1/3: at ~0.5 um pitch each cell gets ~100+ fF, enough for near-refresh-free retention or 3-bit multilevel storage; density is far below commodity DRAM, so it targets low-refresh, U.S.-made niche memory with zero fab capex.

title: Tantalum-capacitor anodic forming grows high-k dielectric in a beaker
idea: Borrowed from tantalum and niobium electrolytic capacitors, which 'form' their dielectric by anodizing porous metal at a set voltage, giving perfectly conformal oxide at ~1.5-2 nm/V: line storage holes with Nb or Ti, anodize at 2-4 V in a wafer-scale electrolyte cell a 10-person team can build, self-limiting Nb2O5/TiO2 (k 40-80) to exact thickness, then fill the top electrode.
why: Fact 1 and capex: conformality does not depend on aspect ratio, the tool is a ~$200k plating-style cell, and k 40-80 approaches the k~70 target; leakage of anodic films is the risk.

title: Pressure-cooker deuterium anneal to upgrade leaky DRAM wafers
idea: Borrowed from pressure cookers, which speed cooking with pressure: a small team runs a 20 atm deuterium furnace at ~400 C on retention-fallout DRAM wafers, driving D into the Si/SiO2 interface traps behind the leakage tail (Si-D bonds resist breaking far better than Si-H), then re-tests and re-bins them.
why: Fact 3: shrinking the leakage tail can stretch refresh 2-4x and rescue otherwise scrapped die; a high-pressure anneal vessel is a modest, small-team-buildable tool.

title: Certified pre-owned DRAM: re-profiled hyperscaler memory with warranty
idea: Borrowed from certified pre-owned cars: a 10-person shop buys DIMMs from retired cloud servers by the ton, runs 48-hour retention, row-hammer and temperature profiling on FPGA test rigs, rewrites each DIMM's SPD with measured timing and refresh bins, swaps weak chips and sells warrantied modules for CXL memory expanders.
why: Supply: millions of DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs retire yearly; reuse adds supply with zero wafer capacity at ~30-50% of new price.

title: Record-pressing father-mother-son electroforming multiplies nanoimprint stamps
idea: Borrowed from vinyl pressing, which electroforms a nickel 'father' from the lacquer master, then 'mothers', then hundreds of 'son' stampers: a 10-person shop takes one e-beam quartz master per DRAM array layer, electroforms nickel generations and casts UV-cured hybrid-polymer working stamps, selling cheap daughter templates to NIL fabs.
why: Fact 4: NIL cost is dominated by template price and wear; daughter replication can cut template cost per wafer 10-100x. Defect amplification across generations is the risk.

title: Black-silicon MacEtch: catalytic wet etching of 100:1 capacitor holes
idea: Borrowed from solar black-silicon texturing, where Ag/Au catalyst sinks into silicon in HF/H2O2 and drills vertical pores: deposit an amorphous-Si capacitor mold, pattern a thin gold mesh on the hole lattice, immerse so the catalyst etches straight down to AR >100 at room temperature, strip the gold and line with electrode and dielectric; a small team runs it on a wet bench.
why: Facts 1/4: replaces a $10M+ high-AR plasma etcher with a ~$100k wet bench and has no aspect-ratio-dependent slowdown; gold contamination and verticality control are risks.

title: Perovskite-solar ink chemistry for k-70 capacitor dielectrics
idea: Borrowed from perovskite-solar labs, which make films by spin-coating inks and low-temperature anneals: infiltrate Ba-Sr-Ti alkoxide inks into storage holes with supercritical-CO2 assist, then crystallize the BST (k 70-150) by flash-lamp photonic curing, all in a glovebox-scale line a 10-person team can run.
why: Fact 1: a k jump allows AR ~50 instead of 115 without a $5M ALD tool; conformal infiltration into 20 nm holes and leakage at nm thickness are high risk.

title: Moveable-type reticles: compose new periphery masks from tile library
idea: Borrowed from Gutenberg's moveable type: keep a library of reticles holding standard periphery 'glyphs' (sense-amp strip, row decoder, I/O cell, fuse bank), and a 10-person team writes the compositor that exposes each chip variant as a stitched multi-shot layout, so new DRAM organizations need zero new masks on non-array layers.
why: Facts 4/7: mask sets cost $5-15M and freeze designs; tile composition makes low-volume U.S. DRAM variants viable at a ~20-30% throughput cost on non-critical layers.

title: Weather-balloon swap: hydrogen backside gas replaces helium in chucks
idea: Borrowed from weather services that fly hydrogen instead of scarce helium: H2 conducts heat about as well as or better than He, so a small team builds a retrofit gas panel feeding 5-20 Torr electrolytic H2 to electrostatic-chuck backside cooling, with N2 sheath, ppm leak sensing and interlocks, qualifying tool by tool.
why: Scarce resource: backside cooling is a top fab helium use and ~30% of helium supply is offline since March 2026; H2 diffusion into devices and safety qualification are the risks.

title: MRI zero-boil-off approach: helium recapture skids for fab tools
idea: Borrowed from modern MRI magnets, which lose almost no helium because a cryocooler recondenses boil-off: a small team builds bolt-on skids that collect helium from chuck backside, leak-check and purge exhausts, run it through a membrane separator, pressure-swing adsorber and cryo-purifier, and return 6N helium to the tool manifold.
why: Scarce resource: recapturing 70-90% of fab helium shields DRAM output from the Qatar outage for roughly $1M per fab.

title: Precious-metal streaming finance for DRAM wafer starts
idea: Borrowed from royalty-streaming firms like Franco-Nevada, which fund mines upfront for a fixed share of future metal at a fixed low price with a small staff: a 10-person fund pays ~20% of a DRAM line's capex in exchange for 10% of its wafer output for 15 years at cash cost, and resells the bits on long-term contracts to hyperscalers.
why: Capital intensity: non-dilutive, non-debt capex lowers the cost of capital for new fabs and gives buyers a hedge against 4x price spikes.

title: Airbnb for idle cleanroom tools: memory prototyping by the hour
idea: Borrowed from Airbnb monetizing spare rooms: a 10-person team builds a booking, recipe-transfer and wafer-logistics platform over idle tool hours in U.S. university, national-lab and 200 mm commercial cleanrooms, so memory startups route split lots across ALD at one site, etch at another and test at a third.
why: Capital and time: a new cell concept today needs a ~$50M pilot line; renting tool hours gives 10-50x cheaper, faster learning cycles on U.S. soil.

title: Display demura for DRAM: ship per-die retention maps, relax specs
idea: Borrowed from OLED panels, which are cheap only because every pixel's mura is measured and a correction table is burned into the driver: at wafer probe, record each die's weak-row retention map (a few KB), store it in module SPD/flash, and have the controller refresh weak rows fast and strong rows 4-8x slower, so fabs can ship die with looser leakage specs; firmware and test software fit a small team.
why: Facts 3/4: a relaxed leakage-tail spec raises yield and skips process tightening; refresh energy drops ~50-70%.

title: Pharma plate screening: composition-spread capacitor libraries on one wafer
idea: Borrowed from drug discovery, which screens thousands of compounds in parallel plates: co-sputter from three targets to make continuous composition gradients (Ti-Zr-Al-O, Sr-Ti-Nb-O) across one wafer, shadow-mask 10,000 MIM capacitor dots, and auto-probe k, leakage and breakdown overnight with one sputter tool and a probe station.
why: Fact 1: finds k~70 low-leakage dielectrics ~100x faster than one composition per wafer, inside a 10-person budget.

title: Liberty-ship DRAM: frozen open design built by many fabs
idea: Borrowed from WWII Liberty ships, one frozen simplified design built in 18 yards by non-specialists: a 10-person federal program office freezes a royalty-free 8 Gb DDR4-class 1T1C design on ~25 nm DUV with documented recipes and test programs, and licenses it with qualification support to any U.S. fab or foundry.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: removes the ~$500M+ design and IP barrier that keeps foundries out of commodity DRAM and creates surge capacity for critical supply.

title: Linux-style open DRAM compiler on U.S. open PDKs
idea: Borrowed from open-source software turning OS kernels into a commons: a 10-person team builds an OpenRAM-like generator for gain-cell and 1T1C eDRAM macros on the SkyWater 130 nm and GlobalFoundries 180 nm open PDKs, emitting layout, sense amps, refresh controller and characterization so any ASIC team embeds MBs of dense memory instead of buying discrete DRAM.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply: moves some IoT, edge and defense demand off commodity DRAM onto memory made in U.S. foundries, at ~2-3x SRAM density.

title: Nespresso pods: sealed precursor cartridges for micro-fab ALD
idea: Borrowed from coffee pods that made espresso possible without a barista: package each ALD precursor (TEMAZ, TMA, TiCl4) in sealed, barcoded, heated single-use cartridges with built-in vapor regulation that click into a tool manifold, so a small fab skips bulk chemical delivery, gas cabinets and abatement plumbing.
why: Capital: bulk specialty-chemical systems are ~10% of fab capex and months of build; cartridges let small U.S. pilot fabs start in weeks.

title: Plasmonics nanosphere lithography: floated monolayer masks for capacitor arrays
idea: Borrowed from plasmonics labs, which float colloidal spheres into a close-packed monolayer on water and lift it onto a substrate: float 40 nm monodisperse silica spheres on a Langmuir-Blodgett trough over a wafer with shallow lattice guides, shrink them by plasma, and use them as the etch mask for the hexagonal storage-node array.
why: Fact 4: replaces an EUV layer with a ~$50k trough a small team can run; the honeycomb matches DRAM's capacitor lattice; grain-boundary defects are the high risk.

title: Controlled spalling from PV: peel device layers, reuse substrates tenfold
idea: Borrowed from IBM's solar controlled-spalling work, which peels 10-20 um silicon layers by plating a stressed nickel film and starting a crack: a small team spalls blank device layers off 300 mm substrates for epi or bonding, mounts them on cheap carriers and re-polishes the donor wafer for 5-10 reuses.
why: Scarce resource: cuts crystal growth, HPQ crucible and polysilicon demand per bit 5-10x and yields thin dies for stacking; surface roughness and crack control are risks.

title: PCB electroless plating replaces tungsten CVD contact plugs
idea: Borrowed from PCB through-hole metallization, which plates millions of holes with no vacuum: seed DRAM bitline-contact and landing-plug holes with a Pd-activated monolayer, then electroless-plate cobalt or nickel-boron bottom-up on a wet bench, replacing WF6 CVD tungsten.
why: Scarce resource and capex: removes tungsten (China ~80%) and WF6 CVD tools; a plating bench costs ~1/10 of CVD; resistivity and voiding still need proof.

title: OLED fine-metal-mask evaporation: resistless shadow patterning of thick metals
idea: Borrowed from OLED fabs, which pattern pixels by evaporating through fine metal masks with no photoresist: pattern DRAM's coarse top-metal, power grid and redistribution layers (>3 um lines) by depositing through reusable Invar shadow masks on a small-team-built aligner, deleting coat, expose, develop, etch and strip for those levels.
why: Fact 4: removes 3-5 litho loops per wafer on non-critical layers, roughly 5-8% of process steps and their tools.

title: Actuarial adaptive test: warranty-priced risk replaces blanket burn-in
idea: Borrowed from insurers, who price risk statistically instead of inspecting every customer: a small team builds a model using each die's inline and probe parametrics to predict field-failure probability, skips long burn-in and retention screens for the low-risk ~80%, and backs the shipped population with a priced warranty reserve.
why: Capital: DRAM test and burn-in is ~10-15% of back-end capex and a throughput bottleneck; adaptive test can cut tester-hours 30-50%.

title: Shrinky Dinks lithography: pattern large, heat-shrink into imprint masters
idea: Borrowed from the Shrinky Dinks toy, whose pre-stretched polystyrene shrinks ~2.5x when baked: write DRAM array master patterns oversized on pre-stretched shape-memory polymer with cheap optical lithography, shrink thermally, electroform a hard nickel copy as a NIL master, and repeat for a second shrink stage, all in a garage-scale lab.
why: Fact 4: master fabrication without e-beam or EUV; edge roughness and non-uniform shrink below 50 nm make it speculative.
